\chapter{El reparto}
\label{ch:es-reparto}
\hlchaptermodality{452}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can deal with a delivery: read the card left through the door, say where the parcel has gone, quote a tracking number, and ask for a time that suits me.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el almacén]{el almacén — where the boxes wait}

\label{lesson:ES-C452-almacen}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la tienda} and \textbf{la caja}. The shop sells them; somewhere else keeps them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el almacén}
\textbf{el almacén} — the warehouse, and in a shop the stockroom out the back.

\emph{Está en el almacén} — it's in the stockroom. \emph{No queda en almacén} — there's none left in stock. \emph{Los almacenes} — the plural, and note the accent disappears: \emph{almacén} needs it, \emph{almacenes} does not.

\textbf{Almacenar} is the verb, to store. A computer stores the same way: \emph{datos almacenados}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the accent that comes and goes}]
The stress never moves. The mark does:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{singular} & \textbf{plural} \\
\midrule
el almac\textbf{é}n & los almac\textbf{e}nes \\
el exam\textbf{e}n $\to$ & los ex\textbf{á}menes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Almacén} ends in \textbf{n} with the stress on the last syllable, which is not the default, so it needs a mark. Add \emph{-es} and the stress is now on the second-to-last syllable, which \textbf{is} the default — so the mark comes off.

\emph{Examen} runs the opposite way for the same reason, and having the two side by side is the clearest way to see that the accent is a correction to a rule, not a property of the word.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Arabic \textbf{al-makhzan}, the storehouse — from \emph{khazana}, to store up.

The \textbf{al-} is the Arabic definite article, and Spanish swallowed it whole. That happened to hundreds of words during the centuries of Arabic rule, and once you know the sign you can spot them: \emph{almohada}, \emph{alcalde}, \emph{alfombra}, \emph{algodón}, \emph{azúcar}, \emph{aceite}. Every \emph{al-} at the front of a Spanish word is worth a second look.

So \emph{el almacén} is, strictly, \textquotedblleft{}the the-storehouse\textquotedblright{}. Spanish was not troubled by this and neither is English, which took \emph{magazine} from the same Arabic word by way of French — a store of articles, and then a store of ammunition.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item it's in the stockroom
  \item the plural, and say whether it keeps the accent
  \item what the \emph{al-} at the front is
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The warehouse? (\textbf{El almacén}.) The plural? (\textbf{Los almacenes}, no accent.) Which English word is its cousin? (\textbf{Magazine}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la ruta]{la ruta — the way through}

\label{lesson:ES-C452-ruta}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{roto} and \textbf{la calle}. One of those two is about to turn up inside a word for a road.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la ruta}
\textbf{la ruta} — the route.

\emph{La ruta del reparto} — the delivery round. \emph{Cambiar de ruta} — to change route. \emph{La ruta más corta} — the shortest way. \emph{En ruta} — on the way.

It is the word for a \textbf{planned} road, which is why a delivery driver, a bus company and a hiking map all use it. The street itself stays \emph{la calle}; the line you trace across several of them is \emph{la ruta}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: ruta, camino, calle}]
Three words an English speaker would cover with \textquotedblleft{}road\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}way\textquotedblright{}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what it is} & \textbf{the word} \\
\midrule
the street with the houses on it & \textbf{la calle} \\
the path underfoot & \textbf{el camino} \\
the plan of where to go & \textbf{la ruta} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Voy por la calle Mayor} — I'm going along a particular street. \emph{El camino está mojado} — the path is wet, something you can stand on. \emph{La ruta pasa por tres pueblos} — the route goes through three villages, which is a fact about the plan and not about any surface.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{via rupta} — a \textbf{broken} way.

\emph{Rupta} is the participle of \emph{rumpere}, to burst or break, and it is the very word you already have in \textbf{roto}. A \emph{via rupta} was a road forced through what was in the way: trees felled, rock broken, a line opened where there had been none.

Latin then dropped the \emph{via} and kept the adjective, which is how a word meaning \textquotedblleft{}broken\textquotedblright{} ended up meaning \textquotedblleft{}route\textquotedblright{}. English took it from French as \textbf{route}, and also as \textbf{rout} — an army broken open — and \textbf{routine}, a way so well worn that you no longer choose it.

So \emph{roto} and \emph{ruta} are one word. A broken plate and a road through a mountain are the same idea applied to two different obstacles.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the delivery route leaves from the warehouse
  \item we have to change route
  \item what \emph{roto} and \emph{ruta} have in common
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The route? (\textbf{La ruta}.) The street? (\textbf{La calle}.) What did \emph{via rupta} mean? (\textbf{A broken way} — forced through.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el seguimiento]{el seguimiento — where the parcel is}

\label{lesson:ES-C452-seguimiento}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{seguir} and \textbf{el entrenamiento}. Put the ending of the second onto the first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el seguimiento}
\textbf{el seguimiento} — tracking, and in a clinic or an office, follow-up.

\emph{El número de seguimiento} — the tracking number. \emph{Hacer seguimiento de un pedido} — to track an order. \emph{Una consulta de seguimiento} — a follow-up appointment.

Whatever is being followed, the word is the same: a parcel across a country, a patient across six months, a complaint across three departments.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: you could have built this yourself}]
\textbf{Seguir} you have had for chapters. \textbf{-miento} you met on \emph{entrenamiento}. Put them together and the word comes out with its gender attached:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{noun} \\
\midrule
entrenar & el entrena\textbf{miento} \\
seguir & el segui\textbf{miento} \\
sentir & el senti\textbf{miento} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Masculine, all of them, as every \textbf{-miento} noun is. And note what happened to the stem: \emph{seguir} has an \textbf{i} that \emph{sigo} turns into... nothing you need here, because \textbf{-miento} attaches to the calm form of the verb, not the shouting one.

This is the point at which Spanish vocabulary starts paying compound interest. A verb plus a known ending is not a new word to learn; it is two things you own, joined.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{sequi}, to follow. It is a root you have been walking past for a long time.

\textbf{Enseguida} — \emph{en seguida}, \textquotedblleft{}in following\textquotedblright{} — is next-thing-along turned into right-away. And the family in English is enormous: a \textbf{sequence} is things following each other, a \textbf{consequence} is what follows from something, a \textbf{sequel} follows a film, and a \textbf{second} is the one that follows the first.

\emph{Perseguir} is to follow all the way through, and \emph{conseguir} — to get hold of something — is to follow it until you have it. Spanish named succeeding after the chasing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the tracking number
  \item I'm going to track the order
  \item which verb is inside \emph{enseguida}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Tracking? (\textbf{El seguimiento}.) What gender do \emph{-miento} nouns take? (\textbf{Masculine}.) What does Latin \emph{sequi} mean? (\textbf{To follow}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cómodo]{cómodo — comfortable, and convenient}

\label{lesson:ES-C452-comodo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el modo} and \textbf{duro}. A hard mattress and a comfortable one are about to be the same question.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cómodo}
\textbf{cómodo} — comfortable, and also convenient.

\emph{Un sillón muy cómodo} — a very comfortable armchair. \emph{¿Estás cómodo?} — are you comfortable? And the other half: \emph{una ruta más cómoda} — an easier route. \emph{A la hora que te sea más cómoda} — whenever suits you best.

So it covers both the cushion and the convenience, where English needs two words. \textbf{La comodidad} is the noun, and \textbf{incómodo} the opposite, for a chair and for a silence alike.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the false friend runs one way only}]
English \textbf{commodious} means roomy, and that is not what \emph{cómodo} means. The trap is worth naming because it is asymmetric:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you want to say} & \textbf{Spanish} \\
\midrule
a comfortable chair & \emph{una silla c\textbf{ó}moda} \\
a convenient time & \emph{una hora c\textbf{ó}moda} \\
a roomy flat & \emph{un piso \textbf{amplio}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Going from Spanish to English, \emph{cómodo} is safe — \textquotedblleft{}comfortable\textquotedblright{} is nearly always right. Going the other way, \textquotedblleft{}commodious\textquotedblright{} will not get you there and \emph{amplio} will.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{commodus}: \textbf{com-}, with, plus \textbf{modus}, a measure — the same \emph{modus} inside \textbf{el modo}.

Something \emph{commodus} was \textquotedblleft{}with measure\textquotedblright{}: the right size, fitted to its purpose, neither too much nor too little. From there the road to \textquotedblleft{}comfortable\textquotedblright{} is short, because a thing that fits is a thing that does not chafe.

The measuring sense survives in English \textbf{accommodate}, to make something fit, and in \textbf{commodity}, which began as a thing that suited you before it meant a sack of wheat. Spanish keeps the plainest version: a chair that fits you is \emph{cómodo}, and so is a time that fits your day.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a very comfortable armchair
  \item whenever suits you best
  \item which Spanish word you would use for a roomy flat
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Comfortable? (\textbf{Cómodo}.) What is the \emph{modus} inside it? (\textbf{A measure} — a thing that fits.) The opposite? (\textbf{Incómodo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(el almacén, la ruta, el seguimiento …]{(el almacén, la ruta, el seguimiento, cómodo) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R452-repaso-reparto}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all four: \emph{the warehouse}, \emph{the route}, \emph{the tracking}, \emph{comfortable}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three accents, three different jobs}]
Two of this chapter's words carry a written accent, and they carry it for opposite reasons:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{why the mark is there} \\
\midrule
almac\textbf{é}n & stress on the last syllable, ending in \emph{n} \\
c\textbf{ó}modo & stress three syllables from the end \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Spanish defaults to the second-to-last syllable for a word ending in a vowel, \emph{n} or \emph{s}. \emph{Almacén} breaks that by going later; \emph{cómodo} breaks it by going earlier. Both need a mark to say so, and \emph{ruta} and \emph{seguimiento} need none because both obey the default.

That is why \emph{almacenes} loses the accent while \emph{cómodos} keeps it. The mark is a \textbf{correction to a rule}, not a decoration attached to a word, so it appears and disappears as the word changes shape.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two of the four were already yours}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{new word} & \textbf{what it was built on} \\
\midrule
\textbf{la ruta} & \emph{roto} — Latin \emph{via rupta}, a broken way \\
\textbf{el seguimiento} & \emph{seguir} plus the \emph{-miento} of \emph{entrenamiento} \\
\textbf{cómodo} & \emph{el modo}, a measure, with \emph{com-} in front \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{La ruta} is the one to keep. You learned \emph{roto} for a plate in two halves, and the same Latin participle names a road — because a road is what you get when something in the way has been broken through.

Only \textbf{el almacén} arrived from outside the family, and it came from Arabic with its article still stuck to the front.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{itemize}

  \item the route starts at the warehouse
  \item give me the tracking number
  \item which two of the four keep an accent in the plural
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[Practice]{(el aviso de entrega) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C452-sintesis-reparto}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el seguimiento} and \textbf{el almacén}. The card below sends you to one using the other.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A card through the letterbox. Read it, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{AVISO DE ENTREGA}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Hemos pasado a las 11:40 y no había nadie.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Su paquete vuelve al \textbf{almacén} esta tarde.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Consulte el \textbf{seguimiento} con el número 4471-XK.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Puede recogerlo mañana o pedir una segunda entrega a la hora que le resulte más \textbf{cómoda}.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item where the parcel is going now
  \item the two things you are allowed to do tomorrow
  \item what the number is for
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{A la hora que le resulte más cómoda} is the phrase to take away whole. It is how Spanish says \textquotedblleft{}whenever suits you\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{cómoda} there has nothing to do with comfort — it is the convenience half of the word, agreeing with \emph{la hora}.

Then notice what the card does \textbf{not} say. There is no \emph{nosotros} after the first line: \emph{su paquete vuelve}, \emph{puede recogerlo}. Spanish keeps the company out of it and lets the parcel be the subject. The one place the firm appears — \emph{hemos pasado} — is the one fact it is claiming responsibility for.

And \textbf{consulte} is the \emph{usted} command again, the register of every counter and every card of this kind.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines for a delivery card: say nobody was in, say the parcel goes back to the warehouse, give a tracking number to check, and offer a time that suits them.

Then check yourself: did \emph{cómoda} agree with \emph{la hora}, and did you use the \emph{usted} command?
\end{tcolorbox}
